title: Congenital Gastrointestinal Disease
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the congenital and early-life gastrointestinal disorders that boards test most: esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal webs and rings, Meckel diverticulum, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, biliary atresia, abdominal wall defects with malrotation, and cleft lip and palate. Each one traces back to a developmental step that failed: division of the foregut, regression of the vitelline duct, return and rotation of the midgut, or fusion of facial processes. Questions usually give an age, the color of the vomitus or stool, an acid-base pattern, or an associated anomaly. If you can link each clue to the anatomy that produces it, you can name the lesion and predict its complications.
prerequisites: Foregut, midgut, and hindgut derivatives and their arterial supply (celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries)
Bilirubin metabolism: conjugation in the hepatocyte, biliary excretion, and enterohepatic handling
Gastric acid secretion by parietal cells and the alkaline tide
Renal handling of Na+, K+, Cl-, and HCO3-, and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Pharyngeal arches and the facial prominences

connections.how: Every lesion in this chapter is a specific failure of foregut septation, vitelline duct regression, midgut rotation, body wall closure, or facial fusion.
Pyloric stenosis is the classic model of chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis maintained by volume depletion and aldosterone.
Biliary atresia is the main surgical cause of neonatal conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a route to biliary cirrhosis in infancy.
Plummer-Vinson syndrome ties iron deficiency anemia to esophageal webs, and bleeding from a Meckel diverticulum can produce anemia in a young child.
VACTERL, the trisomies, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and 22q11.2 deletion explain why one congenital defect should prompt a search for others.

terms.def: Congenital absence or complete closure of a normal lumen, so the tube ends blindly or is replaced by fibrous tissue.
An abnormal epithelium-lined channel connecting two hollow organs or an organ and the skin.
An excess of amniotic fluid, often caused by a fetus that cannot swallow fluid or absorb it in the upper gut.
A nonrandom cluster of vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies without one known cause.
An outpouching that contains all layers of the gut wall, including the muscularis propria, as opposed to a false diverticulum of mucosa and submucosa only.
The embryonic connection between the midgut and the yolk sac, also called the omphalomesenteric duct, which normally obliterates.
Excretion of acidic urine despite systemic alkalemia, caused by renal Na+ and volume conservation in severe volume and chloride depletion.
Pale, clay-colored stool that lacks bile pigment because conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the intestine.
The normal temporary movement of the growing midgut loop into the umbilical cord from about week 6 to week 10.
Peritoneal bands that run from a malpositioned cecum across the duodenum to the right abdominal wall and can obstruct the duodenum.
The merged medial nasal prominences, which form the philtrum, the premaxilla with the four upper incisors, and the primary palate.
Green vomitus containing bile, which means the obstruction lies distal to the major duodenal papilla.

sections.title: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

blocks.text: Esophageal atresia (EA) is a blind ending of the esophagus, and a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal channel between the trachea and the esophagus. They usually occur together, in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,500 live births. Both arise in week 4, when the respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut. Tracheoesophageal ridges grow in from each side and fuse into the tracheoesophageal septum, which separates the ventral laryngotracheal tube from the dorsal esophagus. When the septum deviates posteriorly or the separation is incomplete, the esophagus ends blindly and part of it stays connected to the trachea.

Tube coils in the pouch; gas in stomach and bowel
Both esophageal segments blind; no fistula
Tube coils; gasless abdomen; marked polyhydramnios
Esophagus continuous; fistula to the trachea
Coughing with feeds and recurrent pneumonia, often found after the newborn period
Proximal fistula, with or without distal fistula

blocks.caption: The common type explains most exam findings; the rarer types are recognized by whether gas reaches the stomach and whether the esophagus is continuous.

blocks.text: Why each finding appears

The fetus normally swallows amniotic fluid, absorbs it in the intestine, and returns it to the mother across the placenta. A blind upper pouch blocks that route, so fluid accumulates as polyhydramnios. In the common type some fluid can still enter the gut through the fistula, so polyhydramnios is often milder than in isolated atresia. After birth the small pouch fills with saliva, which overflows as drooling and spills into the larynx. The first feed does the same on a larger scale, so the infant coughs, chokes, and becomes cyanotic. A nasogastric tube meets resistance and, on radiograph, is seen coiled in the pouch in the upper chest.

The distal fistula adds two problems. Each breath, and especially each cry, drives air from the trachea into the lower esophagus, so the stomach and bowel fill with gas and the abdomen distends; that gas proves a distal fistula exists. In the opposite direction, acidic gastric juice refluxes up the lower esophagus into the trachea and causes chemical pneumonitis. Tracheomalacia is common because the tracheal wall at the fistula has deficient cartilage and is structurally weak.

blocks.title: From faulty septation to the newborn presentation
steps: Tracheoesophageal septum deviates posteriorly in week 4
Blind upper pouch; lower esophagus joined to the trachea
Fetus cannot move swallowed fluid into the gut: polyhydramnios
Saliva and feeds overflow the pouch: drooling, choking, cyanosis
Air passes through the fistula: gastric gas and distention
Gastric acid refluxes into the trachea: chemical pneumonitis
blocks.caption: Each clinical sign follows from the blind pouch or from the open fistula below it.

blocks.text: About half of infants with EA have another anomaly, most often cardiac. EA belongs to the VACTERL association: vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula with atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects, especially of the radial ray. An association is a group of defects that occur together more often than chance would predict without one shared cause, so finding one should prompt a search for the others. EA also occurs with trisomies 18 and 21.

blocks.predict: A newborn has a nasogastric tube coiled in the upper chest and no gas anywhere below the diaphragm. Predict the anatomic type and the amniotic fluid history.
blocks.explain: Without a distal fistula, air cannot reach the stomach, so the abdomen is gasless; this is isolated atresia (or a proximal fistula only), and because no fluid enters the gut, polyhydramnios is usually marked.
blocks.check: Compare with the table of anatomic types and the paragraph on the distal fistula.

blocks.text: Webs and rings are thin, fixed narrowings of the esophageal lumen formed by mucosa and submucosa. Although they are grouped with congenital disease, most are acquired in adults. Because the narrowing is thin and does not move, it catches a solid bolus wider than the remaining lumen while liquids pass freely. Dysphagia to solids without dysphagia to liquids therefore points to a mechanical lesion, whereas a motility disorder such as achalasia impairs both from the start. A short, fixed lesion causes intermittent symptoms that depend on bolus size, while a peptic stricture or carcinoma causes steadily progressive dysphagia, and carcinoma adds weight loss.
Esophageal webs and Plummer-Vinson syndrome

A web is a thin, often eccentric membrane, usually on the anterior wall of the upper (cervical) esophagus just below the cricopharyngeus. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is the combination of upper esophageal webs, iron deficiency anemia, and dysphagia, seen mainly in middle-aged women and now uncommon. Other signs of iron deficiency, such as atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, and koilonychia, often accompany it. How iron deficiency produces webs is not fully understood; loss of iron-dependent enzymes in rapidly renewing squamous epithelium is thought to cause mucosal atrophy and injury. That chronically damaged mucosa explains the increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid hypopharynx and upper esophagus.
Schatzki rings

A Schatzki ring is a thin circumferential ring of mucosa and submucosa at the squamocolumnar junction (the Z line) in the lower esophagus, with squamous epithelium above and columnar epithelium below. It usually marks the upper edge of a sliding hiatal hernia, and gastroesophageal reflux is suspected to contribute. Symptoms are intermittent: a large bite of meat or bread lodges at the ring, sometimes as an acute food impaction, while ordinary meals pass. Dysphagia is likely when the lumen at the ring is less than about 13 mm and uncommon when it is wider than about 20 mm. A Schatzki ring has no recognized malignant potential.

blocks.text: In the early embryo the midgut communicates with the yolk sac through the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct. The duct normally narrows, obliterates, and disappears. When its intestinal end persists, it forms a Meckel diverticulum: a blind pouch on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum. Because it is part of the original gut tube, it contains all layers of the intestinal wall, including the muscularis propria, which makes it a true diverticulum. Acquired outpouchings such as sigmoid diverticula and Zenker diverticulum are false diverticula of mucosa and submucosa only. Other vitelline remnants include a fibrous cord from the ileum to the umbilicus, a vitelline cyst, and a patent vitelline fistula that discharges intestinal contents at the umbilicus.

blocks.title: The rule of twos (approximate values)
rows: About 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve
blocks.caption: A memory aid, not a set of exact numbers; individual values vary between series.

blocks.text: Most Meckel diverticula never cause symptoms. When they do, the mechanism depends on the tissue inside and on how the diverticulum is anchored.

blocks.title: How ectopic gastric mucosa causes painless bleeding
steps: Ectopic gastric mucosa lines the diverticulum
Parietal cells secrete HCl into the pouch
Adjacent ileal mucosa lacks gastric-type acid defenses
Peptic ulcer forms in the ileum at the diverticulum's base
Ulcer erodes a submucosal vessel
Painless bright red or maroon rectal bleeding, possibly anemia
blocks.caption: The ulcer usually sits on the ileal side of the junction, not in the gastric mucosa itself.

blocks.text: Bleeding is the most common presentation in young children. It is painless because the ulcer does not obstruct or stretch the bowel, and the blood is often bright red or maroon because brisk bleeding from the distal ileum passes quickly, before it can turn into black melena. Gastric mucosa in the pouch takes up technetium-99m pertechnetate, which is why a nuclear scan can locate it.

Obstruction has several mechanisms. The diverticulum can act as a lead point for intussusception, in which a proximal segment telescopes into the distal bowel, compressing its own mesenteric veins and producing colicky pain and currant jelly stool. A fibrous band to the umbilicus can twist the bowel into a volvulus or trap a loop beneath it. Inflammation of the diverticulum (diverticulitis) mimics appendicitis. The distinction to carry into questions is that Meckel bleeding is painless, whereas intussusception is painful.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus that progressively narrows the gastric outlet. It affects about 2 to 3 per 1,000 infants, with a male to female ratio of about 4 to 1; first-born boys and infants with a family history are at higher risk. Exposure to a macrolide (erythromycin or azithromycin) in the first weeks of life raises the risk. Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist that provokes strong antral and pyloric contractions, which is the proposed link to muscle hypertrophy.

The pylorus is usually normal at birth and thickens over the following weeks, which is why vomiting begins at about 2 to 6 weeks. The obstruction lies above the major duodenal papilla, so the vomitus is gastric contents without bile. Vomiting becomes forceful (projectile) as the stomach contracts harder against the outlet, and gastric peristaltic waves may be seen moving left to right across the epigastrium. The infant stays hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting, then loses weight and becomes dehydrated. The thickened pylorus may be felt as a firm, mobile, olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium or right upper quadrant, best felt after vomiting.
Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis

For every H+ a parietal cell secretes, it returns one HCO3- to the blood (the alkaline tide). Normally, pancreatic HCO3- secretion to neutralize that acid returns an equal amount of H+ to the blood. Vomiting removes the HCl before it reaches the duodenum, so the body keeps the HCO3- and loses Cl-: this generates the alkalosis. The kidney normally excretes excess HCO3-, but volume depletion lowers the filtered load and activates angiotensin II, which increases proximal Na+-H+ exchange and HCO3- reabsorption. Aldosterone increases distal Na+ reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+ secretion, and low Cl- delivery limits the HCO3- secretion that intercalated cells use to correct alkalosis. These forces maintain the alkalosis, waste K+ in the urine, and, when depletion is severe, produce paradoxical aciduria. Urine Cl- is low, marking the alkalosis as chloride responsive. Hypokalemia comes mainly from renal loss, with a contribution from the shift of K+ into cells during alkalosis; gastric juice itself contains relatively little K+.

blocks.title: Reading the electrolytes of a vomiting infant
blocks.text: A 4-week-old first-born boy has 1 week of nonbilious projectile vomiting. Values: Na+ 133 mEq/L (about 135 to 145), K+ 2.9 mEq/L (about 3.5 to 5.0), Cl- 86 mEq/L (about 98 to 106), HCO3- 35 mEq/L (about 22 to 28), pH 7.50, PaCO2 46 mm Hg, urine Cl- 5 mEq/L, urine pH 5.5. Step 1: pH above 7.45 with high HCO3- is a metabolic alkalosis. Step 2: compensation; PaCO2 rises about 0.7 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3-, so expected PaCO2 is about 40 + 0.7 x 11, or about 48 mm Hg, and 46 is appropriate hypoventilation. Step 3: the anion gap is 133 minus (86 + 35) = 12, which is normal. Step 4: low urine Cl- means chloride and volume depletion, and acidic urine in an alkalemic infant is paradoxical aciduria.

blocks.predict: Two infants vomit repeatedly: one has pyloric stenosis, the other duodenal obstruction distal to the papilla. Which one is more likely to develop a marked metabolic alkalosis, and why?
blocks.explain: Pyloric stenosis loses pure gastric HCl; with distal obstruction the vomitus also contains alkaline bile and pancreatic juice, so HCO3- is lost along with acid and the alkalosis is smaller.
blocks.check: Compare with the alkaline tide paragraph and the generation and maintenance flow.

blocks.text: Biliary atresia is a progressive, inflammatory, fibrosing destruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts that obliterates their lumen in early infancy. It affects roughly 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 live births in Western countries and is more common in East Asia. In most infants (the perinatal form) the ducts are thought to be present at birth and then destroyed by an immune-mediated attack on the biliary epithelium, possibly triggered by a virus; the cause is not established. A smaller syndromic form, present from early development, is associated with laterality defects such as polysplenia, situs inversus, and a preduodenal portal vein.

Hepatocytes continue to take up and conjugate bilirubin, but conjugated bilirubin cannot leave the liver through the obliterated ducts. It regurgitates into the blood, so the hyperbilirubinemia is conjugated (direct). Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and loosely bound to albumin, so it is filtered by the glomerulus and darkens the urine. No bilirubin reaches the intestine, so no stercobilin is formed and the stools become pale or acholic. Unconjugated bilirubin, by contrast, is tightly bound to albumin, never appears in urine, and leaves stool color normal. A conjugated bilirubin above about 1 mg/dL (about 17 micromol/L) is abnormal at any age and requires evaluation.

blocks.title: Physiologic jaundice versus the jaundice of biliary atresia
rows: Appears after the first 24 hours, fades by about 2 weeks
Persists or appears after about 2 weeks
Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and high red cell turnover
Obstruction of bile flow out of the liver
blocks.caption: Jaundice that persists beyond about 2 weeks needs a conjugated bilirubin level, because only the conjugated form signals cholestasis.

blocks.text: The infant typically looks well and gains weight at first, which delays recognition. Retained bile acids and bilirubin injure the liver, and the histology shows bile ductular proliferation, bile plugs, and portal edema and fibrosis. Liver enzymes reflecting cholestasis, especially gamma-glutamyl transferase and alkaline phosphatase, are elevated. Because bile acids do not reach the intestinal lumen, micelles do not form, so fat and fat-soluble vitamins are poorly absorbed; vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time and can cause bleeding. The fibrosis advances to biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension within months, and without restored bile flow most children die by about age 2.

blocks.title: From duct obliteration to cirrhosis
steps: Inflammatory fibrosis obliterates extrahepatic bile ducts
Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the intestine
Conjugated bilirubin enters blood: jaundice, dark urine
No stercobilin formed: acholic stools
No bile acids in lumen: fat and vitamin K malabsorption
Retained bile injures liver: ductular proliferation, portal fibrosis
Biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension
blocks.caption: The time course matters because fibrosis keeps advancing while bile flow is blocked.

blocks.text: In week 6 the midgut loop grows faster than the abdominal cavity can hold it, so it herniates into the umbilical cord (physiologic umbilical herniation). Viewed from the front, it rotates about 90 degrees counterclockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery while in the cord, then about 180 degrees more as it returns to the abdomen around week 10, for a total of about 270 degrees. The cecum returns last and descends to the right lower quadrant, leaving the mesentery fixed along a long, broad base. Omphalocele and malrotation are failures of this sequence; gastroschisis is a failure of the body wall.
Omphalocele versus gastroschisis

An omphalocele forms when the herniated bowel fails to return. It therefore stays within the umbilical cord and is covered by the cord's sac of peritoneum and amnion, with the cord inserting on the sac. Because it reflects a broad disturbance of early development, about half of affected infants have other major anomalies, including cardiac defects, trisomies 13 and 18, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an overgrowth disorder from imprinting defects at chromosome 11p15, with macroglossia, macrosomia, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycemia from hyperinsulinism, and a higher risk of Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.

Gastroschisis is a full-thickness defect of the abdominal wall beside a normally inserted umbilical cord, usually to its right. Bowel protrudes through it with no covering sac and floats in amniotic fluid, which inflames the serosa, mats the loops, and causes dysmotility; compression at the narrow defect can cause intestinal atresia. Chromosomal anomalies are uncommon, and young maternal age and maternal smoking are risk factors. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is raised in both defects, usually more in gastroschisis because the bowel is uncovered.

Uncommon; intestinal atresia from bowel injury
blocks.caption: The covering sac follows from the cause: bowel that never left the cord keeps the cord's coverings.

blocks.text: Malrotation and Ladd bands

In malrotation the midgut completes less than the normal rotation, so the cecum lies high, in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, and the duodenojejunal junction lies to the right of its usual position left of the midline. Peritoneal bands (Ladd bands) run from the high cecum across the second part of the duodenum to the right abdominal wall and can compress it. The more dangerous consequence is a narrow mesenteric base: the whole midgut hangs from a short stalk containing the superior mesenteric vessels and can twist around it (midgut volvulus). Malrotation also accompanies omphalocele, gastroschisis, and congenital diaphragmatic hernia, because the bowel was outside the abdomen when it should have rotated.

blocks.title: Malrotation to midgut volvulus
steps: Incomplete midgut rotation; cecum stays high
Ladd bands cross and compress the duodenum
Narrow mesenteric base around superior mesenteric vessels
Midgut twists: volvulus
Obstruction below the papilla: bilious vomiting
Venous then arterial occlusion: ischemia of the entire midgut
blocks.caption: Ischemia spans the superior mesenteric artery territory.

blocks.title: Using vomitus color to place the obstruction
blocks.text: A 3-week-old who had been feeding well suddenly vomits green fluid and becomes irritable. Step 1: green vomitus contains bile, so the obstruction is distal to the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum. Pyloric stenosis, with nonbilious vomitus, is excluded. Step 2: abrupt onset in a previously well infant suggests a twist rather than a fixed narrowing that has been present since birth. Step 3: malrotation with midgut volvulus fits both, and it is the diagnosis that cannot wait, because the superior mesenteric vessels are being occluded. Step 4: bloody stool, distention, or shock would signal advancing ischemia.

The face forms between about weeks 4 and 10 from five prominences around the primitive mouth: the frontonasal prominence, which gives rise to the medial and lateral nasal prominences, and the paired maxillary and mandibular prominences of the first pharyngeal arch. The two medial nasal prominences merge to form the intermaxillary segment. The maxillary prominences grow medially and fuse with the medial nasal prominences to complete the upper lip. A cleft lip results when a maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the medial nasal prominence on one or both sides, so the cleft lies lateral to the philtrum, not in the midline. A true median cleft lip is rare and reflects deficient medial nasal tissue, as in holoprosencephaly.

The palate has two parts. The primary palate comes from the intermaxillary segment and lies in front of the incisive foramen. The secondary palate comes from two palatine shelves that grow from the maxillary prominences, hang vertically beside the tongue, then rise to a horizontal position above it around week 7 and fuse with each other, with the primary palate, and with the nasal septum. A cleft palate results when the shelves fail to grow, rise, or fuse. Anything that keeps the tongue high blocks shelf elevation, as in the Pierre Robin sequence, where a small mandible holds the tongue up and back and leaves a U-shaped cleft palate. The incisive foramen divides anterior clefts (lip, alveolus, and primary palate) from posterior clefts (secondary palate).

blocks.title: Facial structures and the clefts that follow failed fusion
rows: Philtrum, premaxilla with four upper incisors, primary palate
Cleft lip, lateral to the philtrum
Secondary palate (hard palate behind the incisive foramen, soft palate, uvula)
Palatine shelves of the maxillary prominences
Cleft palate; mildest form is a bifid uvula
blocks.caption: Lip and palate form at different times from different processes, which is why each can occur without the other.

blocks.text: Cleft lip with or without cleft palate occurs in about 1 in 1,000 births, is more common in males, and varies by ancestry; isolated cleft palate is less common and more frequent in females, whose shelves rise later. Most cases are multifactorial. Maternal smoking and anticonvulsants such as phenytoin and valproate raise risk, and syndromic clefts occur in trisomy 13 and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

Feeding difficulty follows from mechanics. Effective sucking requires a sealed mouth: the lips close around the nipple and the soft palate closes off the nasopharynx so the tongue and jaw can create negative pressure. A cleft palate connects mouth and nose, so the infant cannot generate suction, swallows air, regurgitates milk through the nose, tires during long feeds, gains weight poorly, and may aspirate. An isolated cleft lip usually allows near-normal feeding because soft tissue can still seal. The palatal muscles that open the auditory tube, levator and tensor veli palatini, insert abnormally, so middle ear effusions and conductive hearing loss are common, and failure of velopharyngeal closure later causes hypernasal speech.

integration.text: Embryology predicts the lesion and anatomy predicts the signs. Foregut septation in week 4 explains atresia with fistula, vitelline duct regression explains Meckel diverticulum, midgut return and rotation between weeks 6 and 10 explain omphalocele and malrotation, and fusion of facial prominences explains clefts. The level of a blockage relative to the major duodenal papilla decides whether vomitus contains bile, and whether bile can leave the liver decides stool and urine color. Physiology then explains the laboratory picture: loss of gastric HCl produces a chloride-responsive alkalosis that the kidney maintains because volume comes first, and cholestasis raises conjugated bilirubin and impairs fat absorption.

Pathology and genetics add the associations. Atresia with fistula, omphalocele, and clefts often travel with other defects (VACTERL, trisomies, Beckwith-Wiedemann, 22q11.2 deletion), whereas pyloric stenosis and gastroschisis are usually isolated. These associations raise or lower probability but do not decide a diagnosis on their own. Several lesions in this chapter, such as webs, Schatzki rings, and probably most biliary atresia, are acquired after birth even though they are grouped with congenital disease, so the age of onset and the mechanism matter more than the label.

summary: In the common form of esophageal atresia a blind upper pouch causes polyhydramnios, drooling, and choking with feeds, while a distal tracheoesophageal fistula puts air in the stomach; a gasless abdomen means no distal fistula.
Esophageal atresia belongs to the VACTERL association, so one defect should prompt a search for vertebral, anal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies.

Webs lie in the upper esophagus and, with iron deficiency anemia, form Plummer-Vinson syndrome with a raised risk of squamous cell carcinoma; Schatzki rings lie at the lower squamocolumnar junction and cause intermittent solid food dysphagia.

Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitelline duct forming a true diverticulum on the antimesenteric ileum; acid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileum and causes painless rectal bleeding.
Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes nonbilious projectile vomiting at about 2 to 6 weeks and an olive-shaped mass, with first-born males and early macrolide exposure as risks.
Vomiting gastric HCl generates a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; volume depletion and aldosterone maintain it and cause hypokalemia, low urine Cl-, and paradoxical aciduria.
Biliary atresia obliterates the extrahepatic ducts, giving persistent conjugated jaundice, dark urine, and acholic stools after about 2 weeks of age, then biliary cirrhosis.
Omphalocele is midgut that never returned from the cord, so it is midline, sac-covered, and often syndromic; gastroschisis is an uncovered paraumbilical body wall defect, usually on the right.
Malrotation leaves a high cecum, Ladd bands across the duodenum, and a narrow mesentery that can twist into midgut volvulus with bilious vomiting and ischemia.
Cleft lip is failed fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal prominences, and cleft palate is failed fusion of the palatine shelves; an open palate prevents suction and causes feeding difficulty.

verify: Incidence figures vary between sources: esophageal atresia (about 1 in 3,000 to 4,500), pyloric stenosis (about 2 to 3 per 1,000), biliary atresia (about 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 in Western countries), and cleft lip with or without palate (about 1 in 1,000); confirm the values NABNE expects.
The shares of esophageal atresia types (about 85%, 8%, 4%, 3%) and the share with associated anomalies (about half) differ slightly between series.
The rule of twos is a memory aid; the sex ratio is quoted from about 2:1 to 3:1 and prevalence from about 2% to 4%.

The first-born association in pyloric stenosis is inconsistently supported, and the macrolide risk window (strongest for erythromycin in about the first 2 weeks) is described differently; the motilin and nitric oxide mechanisms are proposed, not proven.
Reference ranges in the worked example are approximate adult-style values; infant electrolyte and bicarbonate ranges differ slightly by laboratory.
The threshold for abnormal conjugated bilirubin (above about 1 mg/dL) follows current pediatric guidance; older texts use a percentage of total bilirubin.
The perinatal versus embryonic (syndromic) classification of biliary atresia and the viral trigger hypothesis are unsettled.
Timing of midgut herniation, rotation, and return (about weeks 6 to 10) and of palatal shelf elevation (about week 7) varies slightly between embryology texts.
The mechanism of right-sided gastroschisis is debated (vascular disruption versus body wall folding failure); this chapter states only the anatomy.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Plummer-Vinson (also Paterson-Kelly) syndrome, Schatzki ring, Ladd bands, and Pierre Robin sequence, or descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: tef-types (the four anatomic types of esophageal atresia and fistula), midgut-rotation (herniation, 270 degree rotation, and return around the superior mesenteric artery), and facial-prominences (frontonasal, nasal, and maxillary prominences with lip and palate fusion lines).
